read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1, 3-6 and Appendices A (empirical laws), B (algorithm), C (implementation); D (sketched linear-regression derivation) skimmed

claims.claim: How a language model's loss on each data domain depends on the training mixture can be derived, not just curve-fitted, by assuming each domain's skills follow a power law with a shared common head and domain-specific tails: the loss splits into a capacity-competition term, where domains compete for a fixed model capacity and so all mixture weights interact, plus a noise term that depends only on how much data the domain itself received, which is what pushes the optimal mixture away from the target toward harder domains. Supported only if, fitted on held-out mixtures of 64 1B-parameter models trained on 17 Pile domains, the full form (5 parameters per domain) has lower mean relative error than every empirical mixing law tested (additive, exponential, BiMix, RegMix), and the capacity-only form (3 per domain) also beats the best empirical law, which uses about 2K + 1 parameters per domain; if the capacity-only form implies the optimal training mixture equals the target mixture, contradicting observation, while the noise term breaks that symmetry; and if fitting error stays low on synthetic data with up to 40% of tail skills shared.
claims.decision_rule: MRE: Eq.3 < Eq.1 < Additive (2.209%) < others on 64-model Pile set; Eq.1 implies h* = w; synthetic MRE stable up to p = 0.4 overlap.

claims.claim: Because its parameters carry model size and data size explicitly, the derived law picks better data mixtures than empirical laws and can choose a mixture for a larger, unseen scale from small-scale runs alone. Supported only if, at fixed scale, the mixture it predicts gives the lowest held-out perplexity among the mixtures predicted by four empirical laws and the uniform mixture in every setting tested (4 domains at 200M parameters; 7 SlimPajama domains at 122M and 310M; Pile-CC loss in the 17-domain setting); and if, fitted only on small-scale runs, the mixture it extrapolates to the larger scale (700M on 16B tokens; 1B on 30B tokens) beats the mixture it would choose at the small scale and is at least as good as the additive law's mixture, even when that law was fitted with runs at the target scale.
claims.decision_rule: Predicted h* lowest test perplexity vs Exponential, RegMix, BiMix, Additive, uniform in 3/3 settings + Pile-CC; extrapolated h* < static h* at target scale; extrapolated h* <= Additive (full-data fit) at 1B/30B.

experiments.text: Derive the model. Setup: extend the quantization model of scaling laws to K domains whose skills have power-law frequencies with a shared head and disjoint tails: a model of capacity N allocates units across domains, giving a closed-form allocation x_i*(h) under similar exponents and domain loss c_i x_i*^(-b_i) that depends on all weights through an aggregate-demand term. Extend projected linear regression trained by one-pass SGD to the same structure: L_i(h | N, D) ~ c_i x_i*(h, N)^(-b_i) + A_i (D h_i)^(-a_i) + E_i (Theorem 4.1). Find the optimal mixture for target weights w by bi-level optimisation with online mirror descent using a closed-form gradient (Proposition 4.2).

Show why the noise term is needed. Setup: the bi-level problem under the capacity-only model. Result: because the inner allocation and the outer objective minimise the same weighted losses, the optimum is exactly h* = w, contradicting the empirical finding that optimal training mixtures differ from the target; adding the data-dependent noise term, which depends only on h_i, breaks this symmetry and shifts weight toward domains with larger A_i and smaller exponent alpha_i (harder to learn).

Compare fitting accuracy. Setup: reuse 64 TinyLlama-architecture 1B models trained on 25B tokens of random mixtures over 17 Pile domains (training loss used as proxy for four domains without validation splits); split mixtures into fitting and held-out sets; fit empirical laws with scipy curve_fit, LightGBM (RegMix) or basin-hopping with L-BFGS (additive law and both proposed forms). Result: held-out MRE / MAE / free parameters: full form 1.533% / 0.034 / 5K; capacity-only 2.064% / 0.051 / 3K; additive 2.209% / 0.052 / K(2K+1); BiMix 2.963% / 0.144 / 2K; RegMix 6.480% / 0.136 / K^2; exponential 6.990% / 0.059 / K(K+2).

Stress-test the disjoint-tail assumption. Setup: synthetic losses where each tail skill is shared across domains with probability p, with and without added Gaussian noise; fit the disjoint-tail model. Result: mean relative error stays consistently low and stable as tail overlap rises to 40% in both settings (figure). The authors argue overlapping skills mainly contribute a near-constant loss as mixtures vary.

Choose the optimal mixture at fixed scale. Setup: target = uniform over domains; settings: 4 domains (Wikipedia, GitHub, StackExchange, PG-19) with 25 mixtures on 200M LLaMA-style models for 8B tokens, cosine schedule; 7-domain SlimPajama at 122M / 10B and 310M / 20B with constant learning rate (data from prior work); 17-domain Pile with Pile-CC as the target; fit every applicable law, solve for h* (cvxpy or L-BFGS), and train new models on each predicted mixture. Result: the derived law's mixture gives the lowest test perplexity in all three perplexity settings and lower Pile-CC loss than the additive law's mixture (figures; no numbers reported).

Extrapolate to larger scales. Setup: fit only on small-scale runs (200M / 8B for 4 domains; 122M / 10B for 7 domains), then plug in the target scale (700M / 16B; 1B / 30B) to compute an extrapolated mixture; compare with the mixture optimal for the small scale and with the additive law's mixture (fitted at 200M / 8B for 4 domains, where its optimum is scale-invariant; for 7 domains, the published mixture fitted on 412M-1.4B models and 4B-46B tokens, including the 1B / 30B target). Result: at 700M / 16B the extrapolated mixture has the lowest test loss, below both alternatives; at 1B / 30B it beats the small-scale mixture and matches the additive law's full-data mixture (training-loss curves).

Note limits of the evidence. Setup: fitting accuracy is measured on one reused 64-model Pile dataset; four of 17 domains use training loss as the held-out proxy; the 7-domain results reuse another paper's runs; mixture comparisons are reported only as single-run perplexity bars and loss curves without seeds; the fitting problem is non-convex and sensitive to initialisation (multiple random restarts). The theory assumes one-pass SGD on linear regression while experiments train transformers with AdamW and cosine or constant schedules.
